Neuroimaging imaging should be obtained in the patient with abnormal neurologic findings or in the patient reporting a "thunderclap" headache. A
Acetaminophen, aspirin, and NSAIDs are first-line medications for treatment of tension-type headache (TTH). A
Consider prophylactic therapy with tricyclic antidepressants for patients suffering over 15 headaches per month or taking medications for headache more than 9 days per month. B

background.definition: Tension-type headache (TTH) is an episodic or chronic headache lasting from minutes to days that is typically bilateral, pressing, of mild-to-moderate intensity, and without prominent nausea. Although either photophobia or phonophobia may be present, they do not occur simultaneously.

list.listitem: There are wide variations in prevalence worldwide, with the highest rates in Europe . Globally, TTH is the third most common disorder, with a prevalence of 26.1% overall (30.8 % for women, 21.4% for men), peaking at age 35-39 .

In the US, the 1-year prevalence of episodic TTH has been estimated to be 38.3% The 1-year prevalence for chronic TTH has been estimated to be 2.2%. The lifetime prevalence of tension headaches has been estimated to be from 30% to 78%.

The 2017 Global Burden of Disease study reported a prevalence of 27% of TTH in children and adolescents aged 5-19 during the year 2017. For females, the global prevalence of TTH aged 5-9, 10-14, and 15-19 was 12.1%, 35.7%, and 35.8%, respectively. For males aged 5-9, 10-14, and 15-19, the prevalence was 11.7%, 34.5%, and 34.0%, respectively.

In a cross-sectional study of children ages 10 to 15 years, virtually all reported headaches, with 33% (61/184) having TTH. Only migraine and more severe headaches (relative risk: 7.93; 95% confidence interval: 2.65-23.7) were associated with lower quality of life, and more severe headaches were also associated with lower grades in school. However, chronic TTH have been reported as nearly absent in those younger than 15.
TTHs were estimated to cost more than 7.2 million lost days of productivity world wide in 2016.

In a Baltimore County, MD cohort of 13,343 people, over 4,200 workdays were lost to TTH. In this study, of the study subjects with episodic TTH, 43.6% reported decreased effectiveness at work, home, or school, and 8.3% reported lost workdays. TTH caused 22% of the annual headache-related reduced effectiveness workday equivalents (a measure of productive days lost due to illness).
A European study found that TTH was associated with a per-person cost of 303 euros yearly (approximately $400).
TTH is the most common type of primary headache.
Chronic headaches are associated with a lower health-related quality of life, for both physical and mental reasons.
Pain limits regular activities 38% of the time when present.
Pain limits work or social activities for 60% of those afflicted.
Both psychological and neurobiologic mechanisms are thought to underlie TTHs.
Factors that trigger TTH are common to those that trigger migraines, including stress, anxiety, travel, cold or heat, sunlight, fatigue, lack of sleep, and not eating on time.
Peripheral pain mechanisms are thought to cause episodic TTHs, whereas central pain mechanisms are thought to be responsible for chronic TTH.

Authors of one study found patients with TTH had greater alteration of supraorbital nerve sensitivity, presence of myofascial trigger points of the lateral rectus, and binocular coordination effects following visual effort compared to control subjects.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 20 studies of fair-to-moderate quality found lower pressure pain thresholds for patients with TTH compared to headache-free control for trigeminal (MD -49.11 kPa, 95% CI -66.05 to -32.17), cervical spine (MD -88.17 kPa, 95% CI -108.43 to -67.92) and distant pain-free areas (MD -98.43 kPa, 95% CI -136.78 to -60.09). The authors noted high study heterogeneity and publication bias.
Pain sensitivity appears to be a mediator between stress and headache intensity.
Nitric oxide is thought to play a role in the central sensitization involved with chronic TTH.
There is little evidence for a genetic impact. However, first-degree relatives have a 2.1 to 3.9-fold higher risk of chronic TTH.
Prophylactic therapy with tricyclic antidepressants is recommended for patients suffering over 15 headaches per month. B

Authors of a systematic review of 22 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) found tricyclic antidepressants moderately effective compared to placebo in reducing chronic TTH (-4.8 headaches/month, 95% CI: -6.63 to -2.95). Amitryptline has been most commonly recommended. Some have recommended beginning dosing at 10 mg, but others report that doses below 50 mg have not generally been considered effecitve. Tetracyclics have not been shown to be effective.
While SSRIs and venlafaxine have been recommended in the past, a Cochrane Review found them not to be more effective than placebo.

Authors of one meta-analysis of clinical trials with 675 patients with chronic TTH, found no significant association between use of botulinum toxin A and reduction in headache number. In the 4 RCTs comparing botulinum toxin A with medication (topiramate, amitriptyline, or valproate), there were no significant differences in headache prevention. Side effects of botulinim toxin can include blepharoptosis, skin tightness, paresthesias, neck stiffness, muscle weakness, and neck pain.
A double blind placebo-controlled multicenter trial found that the muscle relaxant tizanidine was better than placebo in reducing TTH frequency, duration, and intensity.
A 2016 Cochrane review found moderate to low-quality evidence that acupuncture could benefit those with episodic or chronic tension-type headaches.
Trigger point injections with lidocaine into up to 14 separate locations were studied in two small trials and showed a modest effect in reducing TTH frequency and severity.
Limited evidence from a single small RCT found memantine ineffective for TTH prophylaxis.

Patients should be asked about warning signs for concerning intracranial causes of headache, such as headache worsening over time, headache changing in character, "thunderclap" headaches (severe headache reaching maximum intensity in seconds to minutes), headache worsened by Valsalva maneuver or exertion, vomiting, or associated neurologic signs. B
The physical examination should include vital signs, especially blood pressure, as well as a complete neurologic examination, including the optic fundi. B
Neuroimaging is indicated in the presence of abnormal neurologic findings or a "thunderclap" headache. A

list.listitem: History should focus on the nature of the headache to include quality, severity, duration, location, frequency, provocative, and palliative factors; association with menstrual periods, the presence or absence of aura, photophobia, phonophobia, nausea, or vomiting; the use of medications, and whether there are systemic symptoms or comorbidities that could be causing the headache.
The most common diagnostic difficulty is trying to distinguish TTH from milder forms of migraine.

A history of fear of smells, or osmophobia, may be helpful in distinguishing between TTH and migraine. In one study, osmophobia occurred in only 6% of 200 patients with acute TTH vs. 86% of 200 patients with acute migraine; no patients with TTH had osmophobia between headache attacks compared to 24% of those with migraines.
Patients commonly underreport symptoms, so that a symptom diary may help with diagnosis.

Patients should also be asked about warning signs for concerning intracranial causes such as headache worsening over time, headache changing in character, "thunderclap" headaches, headache worsened by cough, Valsalva maneuver, or exertion, unexplained vomiting, a change in cognition or personality, or associated neurologic signs.

Additional signs and symptoms suggesting a secondary cause for headache noted in the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guideline on headache include head trauma within the past 3 months, orthostatic headache, or additional symptoms of giant cell arteritis or glaucoma. They also recommend a work-up for secondary causes in patients with compromised immunity, a past malignancy known to metastasize to the brain or for those under age 20 years with a history of malignancy. Rarely, undiagnosed pregnancy may present with the headache of preeclampsia.

The physical examination should include vital signs, especially the blood pressure, as well as a complete neurologic examination, including the optic fund. Additionally, extracranial structures such as the carotid arteries, sinuses, scalp arteries, and cervical paraspinal muscles should be assessed for tenderness. C

Neuroimaging is indicated in the presence of "red flags", including subacute head trauma, related activity or event (sexual activity, exertion, position), abnormal neurological exam, syncope or seizure, known or suspected cancer, immunosuppressed or immunocompromised state, pregnancy , or 50 years of age or older. Imaging should also be considered if there are atypical features that do not meet diagnostic criteria for specific disorders. See chapter on headache diagnosis for more information on the evaluation of headache.
There is no role for routine screening with neuroimaging, lumbar puncture, or EEG in the evaluation of headaches.
See algorithm in .
Acetaminophen, aspirin, and NSAIDs are first-line medications for treatment of TTH. A
If monotherapy fails, aspirin and/or acetaminophen with caffeine or combination caffeine-NSAIDs have been shown to reduce the severity and duration of TTH. B
If nonprescription medications are unsuccessful, consider prescription NSAIDs, the muscle relaxant tizanidine, or prophylactic medications. C
Acetaminophen, aspirin, and NSAIDs are first-line medications for treatment of TTH.
Authors of a Cochrane review of 8 studies with 5890 patients, found a small effect of acetaminophen for treatment of episodic tension-type headache with a number needed to treat of 22.
A 2015 Cochrane review of 12 studies determined that ibuprofen was effective for TTH, with an NNT of 14 to be pain-free at two hours.

A network meta-analysis of NSAIDs, acetaminophen and placebo concluded that all active therapies were more effective than placebo for acute tension headache in terms of 2 hour pain free rate. Ibuprofen and diclofenac were most likely to be the most effective agent based on the SUCRA score.
Authors of a meta-analysis of six trials found no difference in pain relief for TTH between low-dose NSAIDs and acetaminophen; high-dose NSAIDs may be more effective but have more adverse effects.

Authors of 2014 systematic review of 55 RCTs also found no differences between paracetamol 1000 mg, ibuprofen 400 mg, or ketoprofen 25 mg with NNT for being pain-free at 2 hours of 8.7, 8.9, and 9.8, respectively.

In adults with frequent, episodic TTH who have an acute headache of moderate or severe intensity, authors of a Cochrane review found that a single dose of aspirin between 500 mg and 1000 mg was effective with respect to less frequent use of rescue medication and greater treatment satisfaction compared to placebo.

If monotherapy fails, aspirin and/or acetaminophen with caffeine often provide good relief. In a meta-analysis of four medication trials for episodic TTH, combination acetylsalicylic acid, acetaminophen, and caffeine resulted in more patients being pain-free at 2 hours than acetaminophen alone or placebo (28.5% vs. 21.0% and 18.0%, respectively). Combination caffeine-NSAIDs have also been shown to reduce the severity and duration of TTH.The benefit of caffeine in doses of 130 mg in combination with the above analgesics on TTH relief and shorter time to relief over monotherapy was confirmed by authors of a systematic review. Adverse events reported included nervousness (6.5%), nausea (4.3%), abdominal pain/discomfort (4.1%), and dizziness (3.2%). Caffeine-containing products increase the risk of medication overuse headache (MOH).

Use of medications for the acute treatment of headache for more than 9 days in 1 month (non-opioid analgesics for 15 days per month; ergots, triptans, or opioids: 10 or more days per month) increases the risk for medication overuse headache. Prophylactic therapy is recommended for patients suffering more than two headaches per week.
Tricyclic antidepressant medications are first line prophylactic agents and may reduce headache activity, analgesic use, and headache-related disability in chronic TTH.

A systematic review found 22 RCTs of tricyclics for chronic tension type headace. They were found to be more effective than placebo for reducing headache frequency (-4.8 headaches/month) and the number of analgesic doses consumed (-21 per month). In active comparator studies they were found to be more effective than SSRIs.
A Cochrane review found that SSRIs and venlafaxine were not effective at two months for chronic TTH.
A systematic review found poor quality or conflicting evidence for the effectiveness of muscle relaxants, benzodiazepines, or vasodilators as prophylaxis for frequent TTH.

When compared with SSRIs, prophylactic use of tricyclic antidepressants led to less analgesic use and decreased headache frequency, intensity, and duration. More minor side effects, especially dry mouth and sedation, were noted with tricyclic antidepressants.
The muscle relaxant tizanidine was found in a double blind placebo-controlled multicenter trial to be better than placebo in reducing TTH frequency, duration, and intensity.

In a RCT of 96 patients with chronic headache, 42 with TTH, the anticonvulsant levetiracetam was only minimally effective in reducing headache frequency (one extra headache-free day/month), disability and pain intensity, and was associated with mental health impairment on the Short-Form Quality of Life assessment instrument (SF-36).

Authors of a systematic review found that metamizole (NNT = 4)(not available in the US), chlorpromazine (NNT = 4), and metoclopramide (NNT = 2) were superior to placebo for acute TTH pain. Neither meperidine with promethazine nor sumatriptan were more effective than placebo.
A study randomized 108 patients with migraine or TTH in the ED to IV ketorolac or IV metoclopramide. No difference in efficacy was seen between groups.
There is moderate evidence that therapeutic touch is superior to placebo for headache pain relief.
Patients receiving acupuncture are more likely to have reduced headache severity, headache frequency, and medication use 3 months and 1 year after treatment.

Authors of a Cochrane Review found more participants experiencing at least 50% reduction of headache frequency in groups receiving acupuncture vs. control groups (2 studies: 48% and 45% vs. 19% and 4%) or sham acupuncture (51% vs. 43%) groups. Four trials comparing acupuncture with physiotherapy, massage or exercise were of low to moderate quality and reported no significant superiority of acupuncture.

In a RCT of 90 subjects comparing acupuncture to relaxation or physical training, all patients improved in central nervous system symptoms. Those in physical training had significantly improved minor symptom evaluation profiles compared with the acupuncture group, and vitality and sleep significantly improved in the relaxation training group compared with the acupuncture group.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 studies with 1131 patients with TTN found soft tissue interventions, but not high velocity and low amplitude techniques, superior to no treatment on reducing pain intensity (SMD = -0.86) and frequency of pain (SMD = -1.45), although based on low-quality evidence. In another meta-analysis of RCTs, manual therapy compared to usual care in 518 patients with TTN resulted in improved scores on the Headache Disability Inventory.

Spinal manipulation as part of combined therapy (osteopathic manipulation, manual therapy, or with amitriptyline) was effective for the treatment of TTH with respect to headache frequency and severity, based on a systematic review of 5 small trials. One trial found no differences between spinal manipulation alone compared with soft tissue therapy plus placebo laser treatment.

Another systematic review of fourteen RCTs over 14 years found that, in general, manual therapies were associated with positive results, such as decreased headache intensity or frequency or decreased medication consumption; however the authors cautioned that further high quality studies were needed.

In a small RCT of 30 patients with TTH, trigger point Positional Release Therapy was similar to medical therapy with respect to headache frequency, intensity, duration and tablet count. Neither appeared effective, however, in reducing pain intensity.

Dry needling may be helpful, when added to conventional therapies. Authors of a systematic review of manual therapies concluded that dry needling was superior to no treatment on reducing TTH pain intensity (SMD = -5.16, moderate evidence) and frequency (SMD = -2.14, moderate evidence). In an RCT of 44 patients with TTH, dry needling and friction massage were equally effective in improving symptoms.

In an RCT comparing dry needling in active trigger points in the head and neck with sham dry needling in adipose tissue absent of trigger points in 168 patients with chronic TTH, intensity, frequency and duration of headache were significantly improved after active treatment.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 7 poor-quality RCTs with 724 participants with TTH found miniscalpel-needle treatment more effective than acupuncture for total cure rate (RR 1.31, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.57) but not total effective rate. Adjunctive miniscalpel-needle treatment was also more effective than conventional treatment alone with respect to lower visual analog scale scores and higher total cure rates and effective rate.

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis assessed that while dry-needling does not impove pain intensity in the short run, it may be useful for improving frequency of headaches, cervical range of motion, and health-related quality of life.
There is evidence suggesting that topical application of peppermint oil may be effective in relieving TTH.
Guided imagery was more effective than usual care in one RCT of 60 patients with chronic TTH in reducing headache intensity, frequency and duration.

Yoga may be helpful in patients with TTH; authors of a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs, 2 with patients with TTH and 4 conducted in India, found benefits on headache pain intensity, duration and frequency over usual care or low-level self-care.

There is limited evidence that cranial electrotherapy and the combination of auto-massage, transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), and stretching is effective in providing headache pain relief.
Massage and physiotherapy may have a role in the management of chronic TTH.
The 2020 VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline found weak evidence in support of physical therapy for management of TTH.
In an RCT, cervical flexion exercises were found to reduce tension headaches in patients with forward head posture.

In an 8-week RCT of 45 patients with chronic TTH, a conventional physical therapy program three times weekly with or without noninvasive simulation of the trigeminal nerve in the supraorbital area was more beneficial in improving pain than medication only.
Both cognitive therapy and EMG biofeedback alone or in combination with relaxation therapy have been found to be superior to placebo and pseudo treatment control.

Authors of a systematic review concluded that non-pharmacological educational or psychological self-management interventions were more effective than usual care on migraine or TTH pain intensity and headache-related disability but not headache frequency.

Brief mindfulness therapy reduced headache frequency in one RCT. Authors of a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs including 2 with patients with TTH found no significant improvement using mindfulness-based stress reduction/cognitive therapy on headache pain intensity, duration or frequency, although results were imprecise due to poor study quality.
Among 60 patients with TTH, those randomized to body awareness therapy or aerobic exercise had improved pain severity and headache impact compared to a control group.

Patients with chronic TTH randomized to 8 lessons and practical demonstration of a relaxation therapy called Brahmakumaris spiritual-based meditation (Rajyoga meditation) in addition to routine medical treatment with analgesics and muscle relaxants had greater relief in headache severity, duration and frequency than medication alone.

A systematic review of nonpharmacologic therapy in children found cognitive behavioral therapy (including patient education on managing stress, sleep, coping mechanisms, and pain-related topics, sleep, and coping) to be effective.

Patients should avoid known triggers for their headaches and should ensure adequate sleep and hydration. Psychological sleep interventions significantly reduced headache frequency and headache intensity in patients with TTH or migraine headache based on 4 studies, including one study of combined sleep intervention and drug therapy.
A 2016 review found a lack of evidence regarding dietary and nutraceutical interventions for the management of TTH.

Data are conflicting regarding whether botulinum toxin type A reduces headache severity and frequency in patients with chronic TTH. Authors of a 2012 meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials including 8 trials (2001 to 2009) involving 675 patients with chronic TTH, found no significant association between use of botulinum toxin A and reduction in the number of TTH per month. A 2017 systematic review of 11 prospective and retrospective cohort studies published in the preceding ten years involving 265 subjects. Ten found that botulinum toxin type A was effective in reducing TTH pain “intensity and severity.” The authors determined that the quality of evidence was moderate. Authors of a 2019 systematic review of 22 studies (1998-2016) also found mixed results based on low-quality evidence, due in part to variable study design.

Fifteen minutes of high-flow oxygen reduced pain and slightly decreased need for additional analgesics in one RCT of 204 patients, half of whom had TTH, who were seen in the emergency department (NNT= 8).
Conservative or invasive dental occlusal adjustments may be useful patients with TTH.
Occipital nerve block has been used successfully in a case report to treat tension headache.

Prophylactic medications should be increased in dose until headaches are relieved, the maximum dose is attained, or the patient experiences side effects. Most prophylactic medications should be maintained at the target dose for 8 to 12 weeks in order to exert maximal effect.
Discontinuation of prophylactic medication should be considered after six months.
If there has been six months of good control and medication cessation is considered, tapered withdrawal is recommended.
A calendar can facilitate the assessment of effectiveness and promote medication adherence.
NSAIDs should be used with caution in patients with comorbidities, especially cardiovascular and renal disease.
Abnormal neurologic signs or symptoms; a new, worsening, or changing headache; or an acute "thunderclap" headache are among the symptoms (as noted above) that should prompt neuroimaging.

Use of NSAIDs or aspirin should be considered against the risk for cardiovascular, renal, and gastrointestinal complications, particularly in older patients and in those with known comorbidities. Aspirin should not be used in children.

Medication overuse headache (MOH) may occur as a complication of patients overusing short-term pain relieving medications, resulting in an escalating frequency of headaches. A randomized trial compared 3 strategies: withdrawal, preventive medications, or both. There was no difference between groups. Preventive medications include topiramate 100 mg daily and onabotulinumtoxinA have been found to be successful as adjunctive treatments for persons with MOH.
Patients with frequent episodic TTH can expect to have 30 headaches per year; those with chronic TTH have over 280 headaches per year. B

In a 12-year follow-up study, 47% of patients with chronic TTH improved to less than 180 headache days per year; 12% with episodic frequent TTH progressed to chronic TTH, 41% continued to have frequent episodic TTH, and 47% improved. B
Patients with episodic TTH can expect to have, on average, 30 headaches per year.
Patients with chronic TTH can expect to have 285.4 headaches per year.

In a 12-year follow-up study, 47% of patients with chronic TTH improved to less than 180 headache days per year. Of those with frequent, episodic TTH, 12% progressed to chronic TTH, 41% continued to have frequent episodic TTH, and 47% improved.
Coexisting migraine, not being married, and sleeping problems are predictive of poor prognosis. Frequent use of pain relievers may also be related to a poorer prognosis.

In a population-based study, TTH was significantly associated with an increased risk of restless leg syndrome (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.57; 95% CI 1.22-2.02), especially among patients aged 20 to 39 years.

A 2017 review of the prognostic factors for chronic headaches found insufficient evidence to assess prognostic factors for subtypes. The authors reported moderate-quality evidence for worse outcomes with medication overuse, high stress, poor sleep, and low headache management self-efficacy (HMSE).
It is common for a children and adolescents diagnosed with tension headache to be diagnosed later as having migraines instead.
Patients should report whether they develop abnormal neurologic signs in association with their headache or whether the nature or severity of their headache changes.
Avoidance of precipitating factors is integral to management.
Primary medication treatment is OTC acetaminophen or ibuprofen. Prescription doses can be tried as the next line of treatment.
Other methods used by patients for relief were described in a study of 250 TTH and 250 migraine headache patients, and included sleep, massage, rest, and postural changes.
If using the Headache Impact Test-6 (HIT-6) to monitor patients with chronic TTH, the optimal cut-off score discriminating between improved and not improved is 8 points out of a total of 42 points.

Evidence is lacking for the benefits and harms of all interventions (incluing nonpharmacologic) in pregnant women. Combination metoclopramide and diphenhydramine may be more effective than codeine in reducing the severity of acute TTH. No fetal harms have been reported with low-dose aspirin (low strength-of-evidence).
Do not use NSAIDs in the third trimester due to the risk of prematurely closing the ductus arteriosus in the newborn.
TTH is associated with antenatal maternal smoking, self-reported problem behavior, and being bullied.
There is inadequate evidence to support routine laboratory or lumbar puncture examination in children with headaches.

EEG and neuroimaging are not recommended in the routine evaluation of the child with recurrent headaches. Imaging should be considered in the child with an abnormal neurologic examination, seizures, onset of severe headache, or change in the type of headache.

Physical treatments were evaluated in a systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 studies with 1815 children with TTH. Authors found effectiveness, defined as on reduction of pain of 50% or more, for relaxation training (RR: 3.00; 95% CI 1.94 to 4.63). In children with TTH and temporomandibular disorders, occlusal appliances were effective (RR 2.58; 95% CI 1.37 to 4.85).

In one RCT, children with migraine or TTH who were randomized to 8 sessions of psychodynamic psychotherapy vs. usual care consisting of clinical interview, neurological examination, counseling, and symptomatic therapy had a significant improvement in headache frequency, intensity and duration at 6 months.
